analysis.one_liner: Gives people in managed care plans binding outside appeals for denied care, easier access to specialists, and a right to sue.
analysis.headline: The bill was placed on the Senate calendar in September 2000 and sat there until the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set national rules for health plans: if an HMO or insurer denies care as not medically necessary, the patient could appeal to an independent outside panel whose decision binds the plan, and could go to court over certain coverage decisions. It also required plans to cover emergency care without prior approval, let patients see obstetricians, pediatricians, and specialists directly, pay routine costs in approved clinical trials, stop plans from gagging doctors, and require plans to disclose what they cover and how they pay doctors. It died on the Senate calendar without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of people enrolled in employer group plans, individual insurance, and managed care plans: they would gain enforceable appeal rights, guaranteed emergency and specialist access, clinical trial coverage, and, for the first time under the federal ERISA law, a limited ability to sue over coverage decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in HMO and employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: A denial of care made on medical judgment must be reviewable by an independent external appeal entity, and the entity's decision is binding on the plan or insurer [S3].
Plans must process prior-authorization and appeal decisions on fixed deadlines (14 days normally, 72 hours in urgent cases), and missing the deadline counts as a denial [S3].
An official who refuses to authorize a benefit ordered by an external reviewer can owe the patient up to $1,000 per day, plus attorney's fees, and can be removed from the position [S3].
The bill carves an exception to ERISA preemption so health plan members can bring certain actions involving their coverage in court [S3] [S2].
Emergency services must be covered under the prudent layperson standard without prior authorization, whether or not the provider is in the network [S3].
Patients get direct access to OB-GYN care without a referral, may choose a pediatrician as a child's primary doctor, and can get standing referrals to specialists for ongoing serious conditions [S3].
Plans must cover routine patient costs for people joining approved clinical trials for life-threatening or serious illness [S3].
Contracts cannot restrict doctors from telling patients about their condition or treatment options, and plans cannot pay reviewers in ways that encourage claim denials [S3].
Plans must disclose covered benefits, cost sharing, prior-authorization rules, appeal procedures, and, on request, how doctors are compensated [S3].
If a plan uses a network, it must also offer a point-of-service option letting patients go outside the network [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor self-insured group plans bear the cost of outside appeals, utilization review rules, disclosure paperwork, and exposure to lawsuits; those costs would generally flow into premiums paid by employers and enrollees.

drawbacks.text: External appeals apply only to denials involving medical judgment, not to plain coverage limits or eligibility decisions, and patients may have to pay a filing fee of up to $25 to appeal (waived if they are indigent) [S3].
The outside-network point-of-service option can carry extra premiums and cost sharing that the enrollee must pay [S3].
The new deadlines, review programs, grievance systems, and disclosure requirements impose significant administrative costs on plans and insurers, which typically get passed into premiums [S3].
Opening self-insured plans to lawsuits over coverage decisions would have increased litigation exposure for employers and their plan administrators [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the bill traded modest administrative costs and a capped lawsuit exposure for a real, enforceable check on coverage denials — the binding outside appeal with deadlines and penalties is the core of it. The design is fairly disciplined: appeals go through an internal step first, external review is limited to medical-judgment denials, and the patient's out-of-pocket exposure is capped at a $25 filing fee. The honest cost is that insurers and employers would pay for compliance and litigation risk, and some of that lands in premiums; the honest limitation is that non-medical denials (exclusions, eligibility) stay outside the external appeal process.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with about two weeks left in the session, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar — and it simply sat there until the 106th Congress ended with no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Kennedy introduced the bill on September 15, 2000, with Sen. Daschle; it was read the first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar [S5].
On September 18 it was read a second time and placed on the calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 809 [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no committee referral is shown, no floor debate, no vote — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and self-insured employers ended up better off: no new appeal rights, coverage mandates, or lawsuit exposure took effect, while patients in managed care plans gained nothing from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its only cosponsor were Democrats [S4]; the bill got no floor action in a Senate controlled by Republicans, consistent with the broader pattern in which Democratic-sponsored patients' rights bills moved and narrower Republican alternatives did not pass either.

industries.note: The bill imposes deadlines, outside reviewers whose decisions bind the plan, disclosure duties, and per-day penalties for defying appeal decisions — directly cutting into the plans' discretion to deny care and their administrative freedom. Their gain from the bill dying was keeping that discretion and those costs off their books.

Most employer plans are governed by ERISA, which currently shields them from many suits; the bill would apply the patient protections to those plans and pierce that preemption for certain coverage actions, adding compliance costs and litigation exposure.

Every plan and insurer must contract with certified external appeal entities to resolve denials, creating a paid, regulated line of business — one whose entire function is to second-guess insurer denials on patients' behalf.

The bill bans gag clauses in plan contracts, restricts incentive arrangements that reward denials, bars discrimination by licensure type, and lets doctors advocate for patients without penalty, strengthening their hand against plan controls.
